claim: Neuronal plasticity of the inner retina has been observed in response to photoreceptor degeneration.
source: Neuronal plasticity of the inner retina has been observed in response to photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that references established observations in the field.

claim: Retinal plasticity in response to photoreceptor degeneration has typically been considered maladaptive and may preclude vision restoration in the blind.
source: Typically, this phenomenon has been considered maladaptive and may preclude vision restoration in the blind.
evidence: This statement reflects a prevailing view in the field as described in the abstract.

claim: Several recent studies utilizing triggered photoreceptor ablation have shown adaptive responses in bipolar cells expected to support normal vision.
source: However, several recent studies utilizing triggered photoreceptor ablation have shown adaptive responses in bipolar cells expected to support normal vision.
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from recent literature as mentioned in the abstract.

claim: Whether homeostatic plasticity occurs during progressive photoreceptor degenerative disease to help maintain normal visual behavior is unknown.
source: Whether such homeostatic plasticity occurs during progressive photoreceptor degenerative disease to help maintain normal visual behavior is unknown.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: The study used an established mouse model of Retinitis Pigmentosa caused by the P23H mutation in rhodopsin.
source: We addressed this issue in an established mouse model of Retinitis Pigmentosa caused by the P23H mutation in rhodopsin.
evidence: This describes the experimental model used in the study.

claim: The study shows robust modulation of the retinal transcriptomic network, reminiscent of the neurodevelopmental state, following rod photoreceptor degeneration in P23H mice.
source: We show robust modulation of the retinal transcriptomic network, reminiscent of the neurodevelopmental state, and potentiation of rod – rod bipolar cell signaling following rod photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: This is a primary finding from RNA-sequencing experiments reported in the abstract.

claim: The study shows potentiation of rod-rod bipolar cell signaling following rod photoreceptor degeneration in P23H mice.
source: We show robust modulation of the retinal transcriptomic network, reminiscent of the neurodevelopmental state, and potentiation of rod – rod bipolar cell signaling following rod photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: This is a primary finding from electrophysiology experiments reported in the abstract.

claim: P23H mice have highly sensitive night vision even when more than half of the rod photoreceptors were lost.
source: Additionally, we found highly sensitive night vision in P23H mice even when more than half of the rod photoreceptors were lost.
evidence: This is a primary finding from behavioral experiments reported in the abstract.

claim: The results suggest retinal adaptation leading to persistent visual function during photoreceptor degenerative disease.
source: These results suggest retinal adaptation leading to persistent visual function during photoreceptor degenerative disease.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the study's findings as stated in the abstract.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity is the process whereby the activity of the neuron or neural network is maintained.
source: Homeostatic plasticity is the process whereby the activity of the neuron or neural network is maintained (Burrone, 2003; Turrigiano, 2012).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity was first described in the central nervous system in 1998.
source: Homeostatic plasticity is a relatively new concept first described in the central nervous system in 1998 (Turrigiano et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by a citation.

claim: Various homeostatic plasticity mechanisms have been reported in different regions of the brain, including the hippocampus and somatosensory and visual cortices.
source: Since then various homeostatic plasticity mechanisms have been reported in different regions of the brain, including the hippocampus and somatosensory and visual cortices, using in vivo models and ex vivo and in vitro preparations (Gainey and Feldman, 2017; Turrigiano, 2012; Turrigiano, 2017).
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from the literature with supporting citations.

claim: Binocular visual deprivation triggers compensatory synaptic changes in the primary visual cortex leading to the stabilization of spiking activity.
source: As examples, binocular visual deprivation triggers compensatory synaptic changes in the primary visual cortex leading to the stabilization of spiking activity (Desai et al., 2002; Goel et al., 2006; Goel and Lee, 2007)
evidence: This is an example from the literature supported by citations.

claim: Stroke can trigger homeostatic plasticity that is thought to compensate for neural damage and play an important role in early phase rehabilitation.
source: and stroke can trigger homeostatic plasticity that is thought to compensate for neural damage and play an important role in early phase rehabilitation (Murphy and Corbett, 2009).
evidence: This is an example from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity counteracts insufficient activity in neural synapses.
source: Homeostatic plasticity counteracts insufficient activity in neural synapses (Burrone, 2003; Turrigiano, 2012)
evidence: This describes a function of homeostatic plasticity supported by citations.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity works to prevent saturation of synapses that could be caused by positive feedback mediated by Hebbian plasticity.
source: but it also works to prevent saturation of synapses that could be caused by positive feedback mediated by Hebbian plasticity, which is better known for its role in experience-dependent plasticity, learning and memory (Abraham and Bear, 1996).
evidence: This describes another function of homeostatic plasticity supported by a citation.

claim: The neural retina of the eye is considered relatively stable both structurally and functionally after postnatal development.
source: The neural retina of the eye is considered relatively stable both structurally and functionally after postnatal development.
evidence: This is a general statement about retinal biology.

claim: Remodeling of the retina in response to photoreceptor degenerative diseases is well established.
source: Still, remodeling of the retina in response to photoreceptor degenerative diseases is well established.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge in the field.

claim: Retinal remodeling has often been described as a maladaptive process that can exacerbate the disease and impede treatment strategies designed to rescue light responsiveness of the retina.
source: Retinal remodeling often has been described as a maladaptive process that can exacerbate the disease and impede treatment strategies designed to rescue light responsiveness of the retina (Fariss et al., 2000; Jones and Marc, 2005; Marc and Jones, 2003b; Telias et al., 2019; Toychiev et al., 2013).
evidence: This summarizes a view from the literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: Retinal remodeling involves formation of ectopic synapses and expression of disruptive spontaneous oscillatory activity in the post-receptoral inner retina during photoreceptor degenerative disease.
source: It involves formation of ectopic synapses and expression of disruptive spontaneous oscillatory activity in the post-receptoral inner retina during photoreceptor degenerative disease (Goo et al., 2011; Haverkamp et al., 2006; Margolis et al., 2008; Michalakis et al., 2013; Stasheff, 2008; Toychiev et al., 2013; Tu et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes features of retinal remodeling supported by multiple citations.

claim: Recent evidence supports adaptive rather than solely destructive neural changes in the retina during photoreceptor degeneration.
source: In contrast, recent evidence supports adaptive rather than solely destructive neural changes.
evidence: This introduces a contrasting view supported by subsequent examples.

claim: Dendritic compensatory synapse formation occurs in retinal bipolar cells when various retinal cells, including rod and cone photoreceptors, have been ablated.
source: For example, dendritic compensatory synapse formation occurs in retinal bipolar cells when various retinal cells, including rod and cone photoreceptors, have been ablated (Beier et al., 2017; Beier et al., 2018; Care et al., 2019; Johnson et al., 2017; Shen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: Rod or cone bipolar cell dendrites can extend their arbors and form new synapses with their correct targets to compensate for the reduced number of photoreceptor cells.
source: These studies suggested that rod or cone bipolar cell dendrites can extend their arbors and form new synapses with their correct targets (i.e. rod and cone photoreceptor cells) either within their normal territory or sometimes outside of their normal dendritic field to compensate for the reduced number of photoreceptor cells.
evidence: This summarizes findings from cited studies.

claim: Functional compensation without any observable anatomical changes in rod bipolar cells was observed after ablation of ~50% of rods in adult mice.
source: On the other hand, the most recent of such studies showed functional compensation without any observable anatomical changes in rod bipolar cells even after ablation of ~50% of rods in adult mice (Care et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited study.

claim: Homeostatic changes in the retina could help maintain retinal output and vision at or near normal levels.
source: These homeostatic changes could help maintain retinal output and vision at or near normal levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies.

claim: The mechanisms, onset and time course of degeneration as well as the cell types in question all contribute to remodeling in the retina, and whether it will have a supportive or deleterious effect on vision.
source: It is likely that the mechanisms, onset and time course of degeneration as well as the cell types in question all contribute to remodeling in the retina, and whether it will have a supportive or deleterious effect on vision.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the complexity of retinal remodeling.

claim: Whether homeostatic plasticity is present during a progressive retinal degenerative disease is unknown.
source: Whether homeostatic plasticity is present during a progressive retinal degenerative disease is unknown.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The authors hypothesized that an inherited photoreceptor degenerative disease that progresses in a moderate manner would promote homeostatic plasticity supporting normal vision.
source: We hypothesized that an inherited photoreceptor degenerative disease that progresses in a moderate manner would promote homeostatic plasticity supporting normal vision.
evidence: This is the hypothesis tested in the study.

claim: The study used an established mouse model of Retinitis Pigmentosa caused by a dominant P23H mutation in rhodopsin.
source: We tested this hypothesis using an established mouse model of the most common form of Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) caused by a dominant P23H mutation in the rod visual pigment, rhodopsin (Sakami et al., 2014; Sakami et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the experimental model with supporting citations.

claim: The study conducted whole retinal RNA-sequencing, in vivo and ex vivo electrophysiology, as well as behavioral experiments in diseased and control mice during the course of disease progression.
source: By conducting whole retinal RNA-sequencing, in vivo and ex vivo electrophysiology, as well as behavioral experiments in diseased and control mice during the course of disease progression
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Rod photoreceptor degeneration triggers homeostatic plasticity and the potentiation of rod–rod bipolar cell signaling that is associated with the maintenance of highly sensitive scotopic vision.
source: we demonstrate that rod photoreceptor degeneration triggers homeostatic plasticity and the potentiation of rod–rod bipolar cell signaling that is associated with the maintenance of highly sensitive scotopic vision.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study based on multiple experimental approaches.

claim: This type of compensatory mechanism may explain why patients with inherited retinal diseases can maintain normal vision until a relatively advanced disease state is reached.
source: This type of compensatory mechanism may explain why patients with inherited retinal diseases can maintain normal vision until a relatively advanced disease state is reached and could inspire novel treatment strategies for blinding diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings' clinical relevance.

claim: The compensatory mechanism could inspire novel treatment strategies for blinding diseases.
source: This type of compensatory mechanism may explain why patients with inherited retinal diseases can maintain normal vision until a relatively advanced disease state is reached and could inspire novel treatment strategies for blinding diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: Retinal remodeling following photoreceptor cell death has been observed in a number of genetic and induced animal models of retinal degeneration.
source: Retinal remodeling following photoreceptor cell death has been observed in a number of genetic and induced animal models of retinal degeneration (Beltran, 2009; Chang et al., 2007a; LaVail et al., 2018; Petersen-Jones, 1998; Ross et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Retinal remodeling has been observed in postmortem human eye specimens from patients with retinitis pigmentosa (RP) or age-related macular degeneration (AMD).
source: as well as in postmortem human eye specimens from patients with retinitis pigmentosa (RP) or age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Fariss et al., 2000; Jones et al., 2016a; Jones et al., 2016b; Li et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a statement about human pathology supported by citations.

claim: The study utilized a well-established mouse model of autosomal dominant RP caused by a heterozygous P23H mutation in the rhodopsin gene.
source: In the current study, we utilized a well-established mouse model of autosomal dominant RP (Sakami et al., 2014; Sakami et al., 2011), caused by a heterozygous P23H mutation in the rhodopsin gene (RhoP23H/WT).
evidence: This describes the experimental model with supporting citations.

claim: The study focused on rod-mediated retinal signaling and night vision.
source: We started by confirming the suitability of this model for our study, focusing on rod-mediated retinal signaling and night vision.
evidence: This describes the focus of the study.

claim: The study followed structural changes of the retina by standard histology and optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging.
source: We followed structural changes of the retina by standard histology and optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging
evidence: This describes the methods used to assess structural changes.

claim: The outer nuclear layer (ONL) and the inner and outer segments (IS and OS) of rod and cone photoreceptors progressively degenerated in P23H mice, while inner retinal layers appeared to remain anatomically intact.
source: and confirmed that the outer nuclear layer (ONL) where the photoreceptor nuclei reside, and the inner and outer segments (IS and OS, respectively) of rod and cone photoreceptors progressively degenerated, while inner retinal layers appeared to remain anatomically intact (Figure 1A–G).
evidence: This is a finding from histology and OCT imaging shown in Figure 1.

claim: In mice, the thickness of the ONL correlates with the number of surviving rod photoreceptors.
source: In mice, the thickness of the ONL correlates with the number of surviving rod photoreceptors.
evidence: This is a statement about a known relationship in mouse retinal biology.

claim: There were 20%, 60% and 73% decreases in central retinal ONL thickness at 1-, 3- and 5 months of age, respectively, in P23H mice compared to WT littermates.
source: We found 20%, 60% and 73% decreases in central retinal ONL thickness at 1-, 3- and 5 months of age, respectively, in P23H mice compared to WT littermates (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from ONL thickness measurements shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The dark-adapted a-wave showed an almost 50% suppression in P23H mice by 1 month of age.
source: The dark-adapted a-wave showed an almost 50% suppression in P23H mice by 1 month of age (Figure 1I,J) consistent with an earlier study by Sakami et al., 2011.
evidence: This is a finding from ERG recordings shown in Figure 1I,J and is consistent with a cited study.

claim: The total count of short- and medium-wavelength sensitive S- and M-cones remained constant even at 5 months of age in P23H mice.
source: The total count of short- and medium-wavelength sensitive S- and M-cones, respectively, remained constant even at 5 months of age, the oldest time point tested (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is a finding from cone cell counting shown in Figure 1K.

claim: ANOVA analysis revealed a modest but statistically significant increase in the photopic ERG amplitude in P23H mice compared to WT littermates at 1 month of age, which continued at 3 months of age.
source: ANOVA analysis revealed a modest but statistically significant (F1,12=5.25, p=0.04) increase in the photopic ERG amplitude in P23H mice compared to WT littermates at 1 month of age, which continued at 3 months of age (Figure 1L).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from photopic ERG recordings shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Cone function started to decline after 3 months of age, and at 5 months of age the photopic ERG amplitudes significantly decreased in P23H mice.
source: However, cone function started to decline thereafter, and at 5 months of age the photopic ERG amplitudes significantly decreased in P23H mice.
evidence: This is a finding from photopic ERG recordings.

claim: PKCα and calbindin staining patterns and intensities appeared unchanged in 1-month-old P23H retinas compared to WT littermates.
source: PKCα and calbindin staining patterns and intensities appeared unchanged in 1-month-old P23H retinas compared to WT littermates.
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Immunoreactivity of PKCα and calbindin decreased with disease progression until 3- and even more until 5 months of age in P23H mice.
source: Instead, immunoreactivity of both these markers decreased with disease progression until 3- and even more until 5 months of age.
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: VGLUT1 staining revealed slight thinning of the OPL already at 1 month of age in P23H mice, and this degeneration progressed with aging.
source: VGLUT1 staining revealed slight thinning of the OPL already at 1 month of age in P23H mice, and this degeneration progressed with aging.
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Intact morphology and density of the pre- and postsynaptic terminals were observed at the OPL in 1-month-old P23H retinas.
source: We observed intact morphology and density of the pre- and postsynaptic terminals
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2.

claim: The count of synapses was decreased by ~20% in 1-month-old P23H retinas.
source: but the count of synapses was decreased by ~20% in P23H retinas.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from synapse counting shown in Figure 2.

claim: The decreased synapse count in P23H retinas is likely attributable to the overall thinning of the OPL.
source: This is likely attributable to the overall thinning of the OPL.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the synapse count data.

claim: Rod photoreceptors in the P23H mouse model of RP are preferentially targeted in the early stage of disease.
source: These data demonstrate that rod photoreceptors in the P23H mouse model of RP are preferentially targeted in the early stage of disease
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and functional data presented.

claim: The loss of rods occurs at a moderate rate in the P23H mouse model.
source: and that the loss of these rod photoreceptors occurs at a moderate rate (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ONL thickness and ERG data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The loss of rods is accompanied with a modest decrease of photoreceptor-to-bipolar cell synapse count but with no change in synaptic morphology at the light microscopy level.
source: The loss of rods is accompanied with a modest decrease of photoreceptor-to-bipolar cell synapse count but with no change in synaptic morphology at the light microscopy level (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The P23H model is suitable for investigating the compensatory network changes that arise during progressive rod cell degeneration.
source: Therefore, the model is suitable for investigating the compensatory network changes that arise during progressive rod cell degeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the suitability of the model based on the characterization data.

claim: RNA-sequencing was used to determine whether the transcriptomic profile of the retina changed in a manner that might provide functional adaptation in response to rod photoreceptor degeneration.
source: We initially used RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) to determine whether the transcriptomic profile of the retina changed in a manner that might provide functional adaptation in response to rod photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the RNA-seq experiment.

claim: At 1 month the P23H mouse retina has matured but has not yet degenerated severely.
source: Because at 1 month the P23H mouse retina has matured but has not yet degenerated severely, we believed this period would be optimum for RNA-seq analysis (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a rationale for the timing of the RNA-seq experiment based on the ONL thickness data.

claim: 2721 genes were downregulated and 2683 genes were upregulated in 1-month-old P23H mice compared to WT littermates.
source: We found 2721 downregulated and 2683 upregulated genes in P23H mice compared to WT littermates (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from RNA-seq shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There were few differentially expressed genes between sexes, unrelated to disease.
source: There were few differentially expressed genes between sexes, unrelated to disease (Supplementary files 1 and 2), and therefore we pooled samples from both genders in the remainder of the analyses.
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis that justified pooling samples by sex.

claim: Numerous photoreceptor-specific gene classes were significantly downregulated in P23H mice.
source: As expected, numerous photoreceptor-specific gene classes were significantly downregulated in P23H mice, such as those related to ciliary structure, phototransduction, and photoreceptor cell differentiation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from GO analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: GO analysis revealed robust increases in gene clusters associated with neural growth and development in P23H mice.
source: In contrast, GO analysis revealed robust increases in gene clusters associated with neural growth and development, encompassing such cellular processes as synapse organization, postsynaptic specialization, glutamatergic synapse formation, axonogenesis, and cell-cell adhesion (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from GO analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: KEGG pathway analysis showed a total of 74 statistically upregulated pathways including those involved in cell adhesion, axon guidance, and glutamatergic synapse processing in P23H mice.
source: Furthermore, KEGG pathway analysis showed a total of 74 statistically upregulated pathways including those involved in cell adhesion, axon guidance, and glutamatergic synapse processing (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from KEGG pathway analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Several pathways associated with cell stress were upregulated in P23H mice, including the MAPK, NF-kappa B, and TNF signaling pathways.
source: As expected, several pathways associated with cell stress were also upregulated, including the MAPK, NF-kappa B, and TNF signaling pathways.
evidence: This is a finding from KEGG pathway analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: ERK phosphorylation was enhanced in P23H mice, verifying the activation of the MAPK signaling pathway.
source: To verify the activation of at least one of these key pathways, the MAPK signaling pathway, ERK phosphorylation was analyzed in whole retina extracts and found to be enhanced in P23H mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNA-seq analysis at 3 months of age revealed largely similar findings as the analysis performed with 1-month-old samples.
source: This analysis revealed largely similar findings as the analysis performed with 1-month-old samples
evidence: This is a comparison of RNA-seq results at two time points.

claim: Upregulations in cell stress-associated pathways were more pronounced at 3 months compared to the 1-month time point in P23H mice.
source: however, upregulations in cell stress-associated pathways were expectedly more pronounced at 3 months compared to the 1-month time point (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing RNA-seq data at two time points shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Top 20 lists of upregulated 'molecular function' GO term pathways at 1 month and 3 months correspond to each other well, and both show prominent enrichments in ion-channel-activity-related gene clusters.
source: Importantly, top 20 lists of upregulated 'molecular function' GO term pathways at 1 month and 3 months correspond to each other well, and both show prominent enrichments in ion-channel-activity-related gene clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing GO analysis at two time points shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Analyses at both 1 month and 3 months show an expected downregulation of photoreceptor-enriched genes due to progressive loss of rods but increases in several postsynaptic transcripts that encode crucial proteins for ON bipolar cell depolarization, such as mGluR6 and TRPM1.
source: Furthermore, analyses at both age points show an expected downregulation of photoreceptor-enriched genes due to progressive loss of rods but increases in several postsynaptic transcripts that encode crucial proteins for ON bipolar cell depolarization, such as mGluR6 and TRPM1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The pattern of regulation of postsynaptic transcripts was confirmed from 1-month-old samples using quantitative PCR.
source: This pattern of regulation was confirmed from 1-month-old samples using quantitative PCR (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a validation of RNA-seq findings using qPCR shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The RNA-seq data show a pattern wherein neural development and growth-related pathways are the highest upregulated transcriptomic pathways in the early disease state, accompanied by persistent upregulations in ion channel activity-related pathways and crucial postsynaptic elements at the bipolar cells, all consistent with neural network adaptation following the initial sensory defect in the retina.
source: Collectively, the RNA-seq data show a pattern wherein neural development and growth-related pathways are the highest upregulated transcriptomic pathways in the early disease state, accompanied by persistent upregulations in ion channel activity-related pathways and crucial postsynaptic elements at the bipolar cells, all consistent with neural network adaptation following the initial sensory defect in the retina.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the RNA-seq findings.

claim: Ex vivo ERG allows quantitative dissection of photoreceptor (RPR) and ON bipolar cell (RBC) responses by using blockers for the metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR) and potassium channels in Müller glia.
source: Ex vivo ERG allows quantitative dissection of photoreceptor (RPR) and ON bipolar cell (RBC) responses by using blockers for the metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR) and potassium channels in Müller glia (Bolnick et al., 1979; Vinberg et al., 2014), see Materials and methods (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This describes the method used for ex vivo ERG with supporting citations.

claim: The maximal photoreceptor response decreased by ~40% at 1 month of age in P23H mice as compared to control mice, and responses continued to decrease thereafter.
source: As expected, we found that the maximal photoreceptor response decreased by ~40% at 1 month of age in P23H mice as compared to control mice, and responses continued to decrease thereafter (Figure 4E, Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from ex vivo ERG shown in Figure 4E and Table 1.

claim: The decrease in the light-sensitive current of the rods precedes rod degeneration in the P23H model.
source: These changes, initially at 1 month of age, were larger than expected when compared to the total loss of rod photoreceptors (Figure 1H), suggesting that the decrease in the light-sensitive current of the rods precedes rod degeneration in this model.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing ex vivo ERG data with ONL thickness data.

claim: Light sensitivity measured as the light intensity to generate a half-maximal response (I1/2) was not reduced in 1- to 3-month-old P23H mice.
source: Interestingly, however, light sensitivity measured as the light intensity to generate a half-maximal response (I1/2) was not reduced in 1- to 3-month-old P23H mice (Figure 4E, Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from ex vivo ERG shown in Figure 4E and Table 1.

claim: At 5 months of age, I1/2 of P23H mice significantly increased.
source: At 5 months of age, I1/2 of P23H mice significantly increased (Figure 4E, Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from ex vivo ERG shown in Figure 4E and Table 1.

claim: The increased I1/2 at 5 months may be due to the contribution from cone cells at this age.
source: This may be due to the contribution from cone cells at this age (Figure 1I and K).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the I1/2 data based on cone function data.

claim: Despite the ~40% decrease of photoreceptor input in 1-month-old P23H mice, their bipolar cell responses did not diminish at any of the light flash intensities utilized.
source: Strikingly, despite the ~40% decrease of photoreceptor input in 1-month-old P23H mice, their bipolar cell responses did not diminish at any of the light flash intensities utilized (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a key finding from ex vivo ERG shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The ratio of bipolar cell and photoreceptor cell responses (RBC/RPR) increased in 1-month-old P23H mice compared to control mice, indicating a significant increase in the sensitivity of the bipolar cells.
source: This ratio increased in 1-month-old P23H mice compared to control mice, indicating a significant increase in the sensitivity of the bipolar cells.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of ex vivo ERG data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Less pronounced but statistically significant increases of RBC/RPR were found in 5-month-old P23H mice.
source: We also found less pronounced but statistically significant increases of RBC/RPR in 5-month-old P23H mice (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of ex vivo ERG data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: These results are consistent with two prior studies showing less severe reduction of the in vivo ERG b-waves as compared to a-waves in a P23H transgenic rat model.
source: These results are consistent with two prior studies showing less severe reduction of the in vivo ERG b-waves as compared to a-waves in a P23H transgenic rat model (Aleman et al., 2001; Machida et al., 2000).
evidence: This compares the current findings with prior studies in a different model.

claim: Analysis of RBC as a function of RPR revealed a significant decrease of RPR,1/2, i.e. sensitization of bipolar cells in P23H mice at all ages tested (1, 3 and 5 months) as compared to WT control mice.
source: This analysis revealed a significant decrease of RP,1/2, i.e. sensitization of bipolar cells in P23H mice at all ages tested (1, 3 and 5 months) as compared to WT control mice (Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from quantitative analysis of ex vivo ERG data shown in Table 1.

claim: The results strongly suggest that rod bipolar cells become more sensitive to their rod input in P23H mice.
source: Since the mouse retina is rod-dominant, our results strongly suggest that rod bipolar cells become more sensitive to their rod input in P23H mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ex vivo ERG findings.

claim: At an older age, it is possible that the cone-mediated responses could dominate and explain the compensation of bipolar cell responses in P23H mice.
source: However, at an older age, it is possible that the cone-mediated responses, which we found to be preserved longer compared to rods (Figure 1J–L), and even hyper-sensitized in the early disease state (Figure 1L), could dominate and explain the compensation of bipolar cell responses in P23H mice.
evidence: This is a consideration of an alternative explanation for the findings.

claim: P23H mice were crossed with a cone transducin-α (Gnat2) knock-out mouse line to exclude the possibility that cone-mediated responses explain the compensation of bipolar cell responses.
source: To exclude this possibility and to study more quantitatively the implications of the P23H rhodopsin mutation in the rod signaling pathway, we crossed P23H mice with a cone transducin-α (Gnat2) knock-out (P23H/Gnat2-/-) mouse line.
evidence: This describes the rationale for generating a new mouse line.

claim: The cones in Gnat2-/- mice do not generate light responses but have no structural abnormalities.
source: The cones in these mice do not generate light responses but have no structural abnormalities (Ronning et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes a property of the Gnat2-/- mice with a supporting citation.

claim: A qualitatively similar phenomenon was observed in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice as in P23H knock-in mice.
source: We observed a qualitatively similar phenomenon in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice as in P23H knock-in mice (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a comparison of findings between two mouse lines shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The maximal rod response amplitude was suppressed by more than half in 1-month-old P23H/Gnat2-/- mice compared to their littermate control mice.
source: The maximal rod response amplitude was suppressed by more than half in 1-month-old P23H/Gnat2-/- mice compared to their littermate control mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from ex vivo ERG in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A further decrease of the maximal rod response amplitudes in aging P23H/Gnat2-/- mice was accompanied by the desensitization of their rods as indicated by larger values of I1/2.
source: A further decrease of the maximal rod response amplitudes in aging P23H/Gnat2-/- mice was accompanied by the desensitization of their rods as indicated by larger values of I1/2 in 1–6 month-old P23H/Gnat2-/- mice compared to their littermate controls (Figure 5A, Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from ex vivo ERG in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice shown in Figure 5A and Table 1.

claim: The rod bipolar cell responses decreased less than the rod responses in 1- and 5-month-old P23H/Gnat2-/- mice before a relatively steep decrease from 5 to 6 months of age.
source: The rod bipolar cell responses decreased less than the rod responses in 1- and 5-month-old P23H/Gnat2-/- mice before a relatively steep decrease from 5 to 6 months of age (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from ex vivo ERG in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The RBC/RPR ratios remained significantly higher up to 6 months of age in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice.
source: Since the decrease of RBC was slower compared to the decline in RPR with age, the RBC/RPR ratios remained significantly higher up to 6 months of age in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice (the oldest age tested, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of ex vivo ERG data in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There was an almost twofold decrease in photoreceptor input required to generate a half-maximal RBC response in 1-month-old P23H/Gnat2-/- mice as compared to that in control mice.
source: Moreover, we found an almost twofold decrease in photoreceptor input required to generate a half-maximal RBC response in 1-month-old P23H/Gnat2-/- mice as compared to that in control mice
evidence: This is a finding from quantitative analysis of ex vivo ERG data in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice shown in Figure 5D-F and Table 1.

claim: RPR,1/2 continued to decrease down to ~20% of that in control retinas in 6-month-old P23H/Gnat2-/- mice.
source: and RPR,1/2 continued to decrease down to ~20% of that in control retinas in 6-month-old P23H mice (Figure 5D–F, Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from quantitative analysis of ex vivo ERG data in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice shown in Figure 5D-F and Table 1.

claim: B-wave amplitudes in the absence of BaCl2 were smaller than those in the presence of barium.
source: We found that b-wave amplitudes in the absence of BaCl2 were smaller than those in the presence of barium (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is a finding from ex vivo ERG experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Barium removes the negative slow PIII component that temporally overlaps with the positive b-wave.
source: This is probably because barium removes the negative slow PIII component that temporally overlaps with the positive b-wave.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the effect of barium on ERG recordings.

claim: B-wave amplitudes were not affected by the P23H rhodopsin mutation in the absence or presence of barium in 1-month-old mice.
source: Comparison between 1-month-old control and P23H mice revealed that b-wave amplitudes were not affected by the P23H rhodopsin mutation in the absence or presence of barium (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is a finding from ex vivo ERG experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Müller cell responses were not affected at dim light but tended to be somewhat smaller with the two brightest light intensities used in 1-month-old P23H mice as compared to those in control mice.
source: Müller cell responses were not affected at dim light but tended to be somewhat smaller with the two brightest light intensities used in these experiments in the 1-month-old P23H mice as compared to those in control mice.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of Müller cell responses shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: These results do not support a role for increased Müller cell activity in explaining the observed potentiation of the b-wave responses in P23H mice.
source: These results do not support a role for increased Müller cell activity in explaining the observed potentiation of the b-wave responses in P23H mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Müller cell response data.

claim: MFA trended toward suppressing the b-wave amplitude but appeared to cause even larger suppression of the a-wave amplitude.
source: Although MFA trended toward suppressing the b-wave amplitude, it appeared to cause even larger suppression of the a-wave amplitude (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from ex vivo ERG experiments with MFA shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Electrical transmission from rods to cones or cone bipolar cells does not contribute significantly to the measured ex vivo ERG bipolar cell component in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice.
source: This result suggests that electrical transmission from rods to cones or cone bipolar cells does not contribute significantly to the measured ex vivo ERG bipolar cell component in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice and cannot explain the observed potentiation of RBC (Figure 5B–C, Table 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MFA experiment.

claim: No significant differences were found in the ERG a- or b-wave amplitudes between the control and treated conditions with any of the antagonists (GABA, glycine, dopamine).
source: No significant differences were found in the ERG a- or b-wave amplitudes between the control and treated conditions with any of the antagonists suggesting that disinhibition, as a mechanism, likely does not play a significant role in elevating rod bipolar cell responses observed in ex vivo ERG recordings from P23H mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from ex vivo ERG experiments with various antagonists shown in Figure 6B.

claim: During rod degeneration and suppressed rod phototransduction triggered by the P23H rhodopsin mutation, the rod-rod bipolar cell signaling is strengthened via compensatory pathways that are most probably intrinsic to the rod axon terminal and/or rod bipolar cells.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that during rod degeneration and suppressed rod phototransduction triggered by the P23H rhodopsin mutation, the rod-rod bipolar cell signaling is strengthened via compensatory pathways that are most probably intrinsic to the rod axon terminal and/or rod bipolar cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ex vivo ERG experiments with various manipulations.

claim: An optomotor response test (OMR) was applied to evaluate behavioral visual contrast sensitivity (CS) in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice and their Gnat2-/- littermate controls.
source: To test if these compensatory changes can promote vision, we applied an optomotor response test (OMR; Prusky et al., 2004) to evaluate behavioral visual contrast sensitivity (CS) in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice and their Gnat2-/- littermate controls (Figure 7A).
evidence: This describes the behavioral method used to assess vision.

claim: The reflexive OMR test was selected to avoid confounding factors caused by potential plasticity in the cortical brain areas that could also promote vision even when retinal output is suppressed.
source: This reflexive test was selected to avoid confounding factors caused by potential plasticity in the cortical brain areas that could also promote vision even when retinal output is suppressed (Koskela et al., 2020).
evidence: This explains the rationale for choosing the OMR test with a supporting citation.

claim: CS decreased slightly in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice only at the dimmest background light up until 3 months of age.
source: We found that CS decreased slightly in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice only at the dimmest background light up until 3 months of age in ambient light ranging from −3.3 to 0.85 log(Cd/m2) (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from OMR behavioral testing shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: At 5 months of age, CS was suppressed at the two dimmest ambient light levels (−3.3 and −2.4 log(Cd/m2)), but not at brighter illuminances in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice.
source: At 5 months of age, CS was suppressed at the two dimmest ambient light levels (−3.3 and −2.4 log(Cd/m2)), but not at brighter illuminances (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a finding from OMR behavioral testing shown in Figure 7D.

claim: A significant drop in performance occurred in 6-month-old P23H/Gnat2-/- mice at all except the brightest ambient light level.
source: In contrast, a significant drop in performance occurred in 6-month-old P23H/Gnat2-/- mice at all except the brightest ambient light level (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a finding from OMR behavioral testing shown in Figure 7D.

claim: A decrease in the sensitivity of rod-mediated vision was expected since absolute rod bipolar cell responses decreased in P23H mice as they aged beyond 1 month.
source: A decrease in the sensitivity of rod-mediated vision was expected since absolute rod bipolar cell responses decreased in P23H mice as they aged beyond 1 month (Figures 4F and 5B; Sarria et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral findings based on the electrophysiology data.

claim: Consistent with the finding that the rod bipolar cell sensitivity to their rod input was potentiated in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice up to 5 months of age, the decrease in scotopic contrast sensitivity was less severe than expected if based solely on the degeneration and functional decline of rod photoreceptors.
source: However, consistent with our finding that the rod bipolar cell sensitivity to their rod input was potentiated in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice up to 5 months of age, the decrease in scotopic contrast sensitivity was less severe than expected if based solely on the degeneration and functional decline of rod photoreceptors caused by the P23H rhodopsin mutation.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the electrophysiology and behavioral findings.

claim: No change in contrast sensitivity was observed in dim (scotopic), intermediate (mesopic) or bright (photopic) ambient light in P23H mice on a C57Bl/6J background with functional cones.
source: In these mice, we did not observe any change in contrast sensitivity in dim (scotopic), intermediate (mesopic) or bright (photopic) ambient light (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from OMR behavioral testing in P23H mice on C57 background shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The P23H mouse line is a well-characterized model for the most common form of adRP, and closely parallels the pathological characteristics of the human disease.
source: The P23H mouse line is a well-characterized model for the most common form of adRP, and closely parallels the pathological characteristics of the human disease (Sakami et al., 2014; Sakami et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the P23H mouse model with supporting citations.

claim: The clinical disease in P23H patients first manifests as night blindness followed by a gradual loss of visual field.
source: Typically, the clinical disease first manifests as night blindness followed by a gradual loss of visual field (Berson et al., 1991).
evidence: This describes the clinical presentation of P23H-associated RP with a supporting citation.

claim: The disease severity and progression are moderate compared to many other types of RP, and the patients can retain normal visual acuity well into their thirties.
source: However, the disease severity and progression are moderate compared to many other types of RP, and the patients can retain normal visual acuity well into their thirties (Berson et al., 1991).
evidence: This describes the disease progression in P23H patients with a supporting citation.

claim: The preservation of vision in P23H patients may be due to the cone population preserved in many patients.
source: This may be due to the cone population preserved in many patients (Hartong et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of vision preservation in patients with a supporting citation.

claim: The maximal rod response amplitude is suppressed by only 5% at post-natal day (P) 14 in heterozygous P23H mice.
source: An earlier study demonstrated that the maximal rod response amplitude is suppressed by only 5% at post-natal day (P) 14 in heterozygous P23H mice (Sakami et al., 2014), implying practically normal amplitudes at eye opening.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: The waveform of the ERG response appeared qualitatively normal in 1-month-old P23H mice.
source: However, the waveform of the ERG response appeared qualitatively normal
evidence: This is an observation from ERG recordings.

claim: The first positive deflection of the in vivo ERG signal (b-wave) as well as the rod bipolar cell responses derived using ex vivo ERG were comparable between 1-month-old P23H and control mice.
source: and the first positive deflection of the in vivo ERG signal (b-wave) (Figure 1I) as well as the rod bipolar cell responses derived using ex vivo ERG (Figures 4F and 5B, Table 1) were comparable between 1-month-old P23H and control mice.
evidence: This is a finding from ERG recordings shown in Figures 1I, 4F, 5B and Table 1.

claim: 1 month of age represents an optimal time for a molecular genetics screen of P23H mice as by this age a functional deficit of the rod population is significant, whereas their degeneration is not yet severe.
source: Therefore, we concluded that 1 month of age represents an optimal time for a molecular genetics screen of P23H mice as by this age a functional deficit of the rod population is significant, whereas their degeneration is not yet severe (Figures 1, 2, 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion about the optimal timing for molecular analysis based on the characterization data.

claim: At 1 month of age the confounding factors arising from any developmental plasticity associated with the retina is avoided due to the full maturation of the mouse retina at this age.
source: Furthermore, at 1 month of age the confounding factors arising from any developmental plasticity associated with the retina is avoided due to the full maturation of the mouse retina at this age (Young, 1985).
evidence: This is a rationale for the timing of experiments with a supporting citation.

claim: If homeostatic plasticity occurs in response to rod cell death in the retina, it must show a discernible fingerprint in the retinal transcriptome.
source: We first hypothesized that if homeostatic plasticity occurs in response to rod cell death in the retina, it must show a discernible fingerprint in the retinal transcriptome.
evidence: This is the hypothesis for the RNA-seq experiment.

claim: The RNA-seq analysis is consistent with the hypothesis that a robust neural network adaptation in the retina takes place in the early stages of photoreceptor degenerative disease caused by the P23H rhodopsin mutation.
source: Nevertheless, our RNA-seq analysis is consistent with our hypothesis that a robust neural network adaptation in the retina takes place in the early stages of photoreceptor degenerative disease caused by the P23H rhodopsin mutation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNA-seq findings.

claim: The light-sensitivity of bipolar cells tended to be even higher in 1-month-old P23H mice as compared to WT controls on the C57 background.
source: In the C57 background, the light-sensitivity of bipolar cells tended to be even higher in 1-month-old P23H mice as compared to WT controls (Figure 4F, Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from ex vivo ERG in P23H mice on C57 background shown in Figure 4F and Table 1.

claim: The higher light-sensitivity of bipolar cells in 1-month-old P23H mice on C57 background may be due to the contribution from increased light responses of cones observed in vivo.
source: However, this may be due to the contribution from increased light responses of cones observed in vivo (Figure 1L)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ex vivo ERG findings based on in vivo ERG data.

claim: Without the contribution of cone phototransduction, the rod bipolar cell sensitivity slightly decreased in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice.
source: since without the contribution of cone phototransduction, the rod bipolar cell sensitivity slightly decreased in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice (Figure 5B, Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from ex vivo ERG in P23H/Gnat2-/- mice shown in Figure 5B and Table 1.

claim: Better preserved visually guided behavior was observed on the C57 background as compared to the Gnat2-/- background.
source: We also found better preserved visually guided behavior on the C57 background (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) as compared to the Gnat2-/- background (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a comparison of behavioral findings between two mouse backgrounds shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The compensatory sensitization of the rod bipolar cells to their rod input cannot be explained simply by upregulation of cone-mediated signaling, since the same phenomenon was observed in P23H mice both in C57 and Gnat2-/- backgrounds.
source: However, the compensatory sensitization of the rod bipolar cells to their rod input cannot be explained simply by upregulation of cone-mediated signaling, since the same phenomenon was observed in P23H mice both in C57 and Gnat2-/- backgrounds (Figure 5C, Table 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing findings in two mouse backgrounds.

claim: The P23H/Gnat2-/- mice were observed to perform almost normally until 3 months of age in a behavioral visual contrast threshold task, even at the lowest luminance.
source: The P23H/Gnat2-/- mice were also observed to perform almost normally until 3 months of age in a behavioral visual contrast threshold task, even at the lowest luminance (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from OMR behavioral testing shown in Figure 7.

claim: At 3 months of age, the overall rod input already decreased by more than half in P23H mice which was expected to significantly elevate contrast thresholds (or decrease contrast sensitivity) specifically at the two lowest luminance levels where the contrast sensitivity is proportional to background light intensity.
source: At this age, the overall rod input already decreased by more than half in P23H mice which was expected to significantly elevate contrast thresholds (or decrease contrast sensitivity) specifically at the two lowest luminance levels where the contrast sensitivity is proportional to background light intensity (Figures 5A and 7).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral findings based on the electrophysiology data.

claim: The gradual loss of the rod photoreceptors, or declined input from them, triggers functional homeostatic adaptation in the retina that allows maintenance of visual function downstream of the photoreceptors.
source: Therefore, it appears that the gradual loss of the rod photoreceptors, or declined input from them, triggers functional homeostatic adaptation in the retina that allows maintenance of visual function downstream of the photoreceptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined electrophysiology and behavioral findings.

claim: Prior research has cast a rather negative connotation over retinal remodeling following the loss of photoreceptors, proposing that it exacerbates vision loss and may interfere with strategies to restore vision in the blind.
source: Our results using the P23H mouse model appear at odds with some prior research casting a rather negative connotation over retinal remodeling following the loss of photoreceptors. Such studies proposed that retinal remodeling exacerbates vision loss and therefore may interfere with strategies to restore vision in the blind (Jones et al., 2003; Marc and Jones, 2003b; Telias et al., 2019; Toychiev et al., 2013).
evidence: This summarizes a view from the literature with supporting citations.

claim: The contrasting conclusions about retinal remodeling could stem from the retinal remodeling phase at which various retinal degeneration models with significantly different rates of photoreceptor degeneration have been studied.
source: We speculate that the contrasting conclusions could stem from the retinal remodeling phase at which various retinal degeneration models with significantly different rates of photoreceptor degeneration have been studied.
evidence: This is a speculation about the reason for different conclusions in the literature.

claim: The rd1 mouse model represents an extremely severe disease where rod death starts at P8 and progresses to practically complete loss of all photoreceptors by 4 weeks of age.
source: The rd1 mouse model represents an extremely severe disease where rod death starts at P8 and progresses to practically complete loss of all photoreceptors by 4 weeks of age.
evidence: This describes the rd1 mouse model based on established knowledge.

claim: The rd10 model exhibits somewhat slower progression of the disease than rd1.
source: The rd10 model exhibits somewhat slower progression of the disease.
evidence: This describes the rd10 mouse model based on established knowledge.

claim: In rd10 mice, the dark-adapted ERG response is observable but already significantly compromised at P18 and by 1 month of age the light responses of rods are practically abolished and most of their photoreceptors have degenerated, particularly in the central retina.
source: Their dark-adapted ERG response is observable but already significantly compromised at P18 and by 1 month of age the light responses of rods are practically abolished and most of their photoreceptors have degenerated, particularly in the central retina (Chang et al., 2007b; Gargini et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the rd10 mouse model with supporting citations.

claim: Functional and behavioral studies using rd1 and rd10 mice, typically conducted with mice older than 1 month of age, may have missed the window for observing constructive remodeling expected to promote retinal output and vision.
source: Thus, it is possible that functional and behavioral studies using rd1 and rd10 mice, typically conducted with mice older than 1 month of age, may have missed the window for observing constructive remodeling expected to promote retinal output and vision.
evidence: This is a speculation about why prior studies may have reached different conclusions.

claim: The slower rate of retinal degeneration in the heterozygous P23H animal model provides a broader window of opportunity for investigating the impact of photoreceptor degeneration on early stage retinal remodeling (phase 1).
source: In contrast, the slower rate of retinal degeneration in the heterozygous P23H animal model provides a broader window of opportunity for investigating the impact of photoreceptor degeneration on early stage retinal remodeling (phase 1).
evidence: This is a rationale for using the P23H model.

claim: Recent studies using the specific deletion of ~50–90% of rods, cones or rod bipolar cells during development or in mature mice have revealed homeostatic mechanisms associated with the maintenance of normal retinal output and vision.
source: Recent studies using the specific deletion of ~50–90% of rods, cones or rod bipolar cells during development or in mature mice have revealed homeostatic mechanisms associated with the maintenance of normal retinal output and vision (Care et al., 2020; Care et al., 2019; Johnson et al., 2017; Shen et al., 2020; Tien et al., 2017).
evidence: This summarizes findings from recent literature with supporting citations.

claim: The results are consistent with the idea that at least during phase 1 of remodeling, photoreceptor death induces functional compensation that supports close to normal retinal output and rod-mediated vision.
source: Our results are consistent with the idea that at least during phase 1 of remodeling, photoreceptor death induces functional compensation that supports close to normal retinal output and rod-mediated vision (Figures 4, 5 and 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings shown in Figures 4, 5 and 7.

claim: Even at the stage where prominent cone dysfunction was observed in 5- or even 6-month-old P23H/Gnat2-/- mice, the rod bipolar cells continued to increase their sensitivity to rod input.
source: Even at the stage where we observed prominent cone dysfunction (Figure 1L) in 5- or even 6-month-old P23H/Gnat2-/- mice, the rod bipolar cells continued to increase their sensitivity to rod input (Figure 5C–F, Table 1)
evidence: This is a finding from ex vivo ERG shown in Figure 5C-F and Table 1.

claim: At 5-6 months, the light responses of rods were already small and the absolute amplitudes of the rod bipolar cell light responses had significantly decreased together with lower contrast sensitivity of their rod-mediated vision in dim light.
source: although at this point the light responses of rods were already small (Figure 5A) and the absolute amplitudes of the rod bipolar cell light responses had significantly decreased (Figure 5B) together with lower contrast sensitivity of their rod-mediated vision in dim light (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a finding from ex vivo ERG and behavioral testing shown in Figures 5A, 5B and 7D.

claim: Up to a point where some residual rod light responses exist, the retina can adapt toward supporting normal retinal output and scotopic vision.
source: These results therefore suggest that up to a point where some residual rod light responses exist, the retina can adapt toward supporting normal retinal output and scotopic vision.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined findings.

claim: Patients at the stage where some residual rod light responses exist might be expected to benefit from various treatments designed to restore photoreceptors and their light responses.
source: In this manner, patients at this stage of retinal degenerative disease might be expected to benefit from various treatments designed to restore photoreceptors and their light responses.
evidence: This is a speculation about the clinical implications of the findings.

claim: The duration during which the inner retina remains capable of processing light signals and therefore is amenable to treatments remains unknown.
source: However, the duration during which the inner retina remains capable of processing light signals and therefore is amenable to these types of treatments remains unknown.
evidence: This identifies a remaining knowledge gap.

claim: Studies with other animal models suggest that corruption of the inner retina would become a problem at later time points, including in P23H mutation-associated RP models.
source: Studies with other animal models suggest that corruption of the inner retina would become a problem at later time points, including in P23H mutation-associated RP models.
evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge from other studies.

claim: Quantitative functional and behavioral studies at later stages will be needed to address the question of how long the inner retina remains capable of processing light signals.
source: Quantitative functional and behavioral studies at later stages will be needed to address this question.
evidence: This identifies a need for future research.

claim: The RNA-seq and electrophysiology data strongly suggest that homeostatic plasticity is induced at early stages of rod degeneration in the P23H mouse retina.
source: Our RNA-seq and electrophysiology data strongly suggest that homeostatic plasticity is induced at early stages of rod degeneration in the P23H mouse retina.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined RNA-seq and electrophysiology findings.

claim: The homeostatic plasticity mechanisms for the increased sensitivity of rod bipolar cells to their rod input remain unclear.
source: Still, the homeostatic plasticity mechanisms for the increased sensitivity of rod bipolar cells to their rod input remain unclear.
evidence: This identifies a remaining question about the mechanisms.

claim: Possibilities for the mechanism of increased sensitivity of rod bipolar cells include (1) formation of new synapses between rod bipolar cells and surviving photoreceptors, (2) increased electrical coupling of rods to the cone pathway, (3) reduced inhibitory drive to rod bipolar cells (disinhibition), (4) pre- and/or postsynaptic scaling, and (5) increased excitability through axonal remodeling of rod bipolar cells.
source: Possibilities include (1) formation of new synapses between rod bipolar cells and surviving photoreceptors, (2) increased electrical coupling of rods to the cone pathway, (3) reduced inhibitory drive to rod bipolar cells (disinhibition), (4) pre- and/or postsynaptic scaling, and (5) increased excitability through axonal remodeling of rod bipolar cells (Figure 8).
evidence: This lists possible mechanisms illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: Hypotheses 2 and 3 (increased electrical coupling and disinhibition) were tested by using blockers for gap junctions and major inhibitory postsynaptic receptors.
source: We tested hypotheses 2 and 3 by using blockers for gap junctions and major inhibitory postsynaptic receptors (Figure 6).
evidence: This describes experiments to test specific hypotheses shown in Figure 6.

claim: The findings did not support hypotheses 2 or 3 (increased electrical coupling or disinhibition).
source: Our findings did not support either of these hypotheses, and it appears that the potentiation of the ERG b-wave is not mediated by disinhibition or altered gap junctional coupling in P23H mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the blocker experiments.

claim: Hypothesis 1 (formation of new synapses) would align well with recent studies showing that cone bipolar cell dendrites formed new synapses with surviving cones after ~50% of cones had been ablated in juvenile or mature mice.
source: Hypothesis 1 would align well with recent studies showing that cone bipolar cell dendrites formed new synapses with surviving cones after ~50% of cones had been ablated in juvenile or mature mice (Care et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2020).
evidence: This compares hypothesis 1 with findings from cited studies.

claim: Ablation of 50–90% of rod bipolar cells during development led to an extension of the dendrites of the remaining rod bipolar cells so that they contacted more rods.
source: In another study, ablation of 50–90% of rod bipolar cells during development led to an extension of the dendrites of the remaining rod bipolar cells so that they contacted more rods (Johnson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Restoration of rod function in juvenile mice, which lacked rod function during development, can lead to the formation of new functional synapses between rods and rod bipolar cells.
source: It also has been shown that restoration of rod function in juvenile mice, which lacked rod function during development, can lead to the formation of new functional synapses between rods and rod bipolar cells (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: The data from IHC staining does not support formation of new synaptic contacts in P23H mice.
source: However, our data from IHC staining does not support formation of new synaptic contacts .
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Fewer mGluR6 positive puncta were detected, reflecting a decreased number of synapses, in 1-month-old P23H retinas.
source: We detected fewer mGluR6 positive puncta, reflecting a decreased number of synapses, in 1-month-old P23H retinas (Figure 2)
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2.

claim: Rod bipolar cell labeling showed indistinguishable staining patterns between P23H and control retinas.
source: and on the other hand, rod bipolar cell labeling showed indistinguishable staining patterns between P23H and control retinas (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ablation of ~50% of rods in a WT adult mouse retina, phenotypically mimicking the situation in young adult P23H mice including compensation of the ERG b-wave amplitude, did not lead to morphological synaptic changes.
source: In line with this, ablation of ~50% of rods in a WT adult mouse retina, phenotypically mimicking the situation in young adult P23H mice including compensation of the ERG b-wave amplitude, did not lead to morphological synaptic changes in the study by Care et al., 2020.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study that is consistent with the current findings.

claim: The RNA-seq data show upregulations in a number of mRNAs of ion channels and G protein-coupled receptors, such as the Trpm1 cation channel crucial for ON bipolar cell depolarization as well as glutamatergic receptors.
source: Our RNA-seq data show upregulations in a number of mRNAs of ion channels and G protein-coupled receptors, such as the Trpm1 cation channel crucial for ON bipolar cell depolarization as well as glutamatergic receptors that could contribute either to the strengthening of individual rod-rod bipolar cell synapses or increased excitability of the rod bipolar cells (Figure 3—figure supplements 3–5).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 3-5.

claim: Postsynaptic scaling and/or increased intrinsic excitability of rod bipolar cells (hypotheses 4 and/or 5) appear the most likely candidates in explaining the functional compensation upon rod death in P23H mice.
source: Therefore, postsynaptic scaling and/or increased intrinsic excitability of rod bipolar cells (hypotheses 4 and/or 5) appear the most likely candidates in explaining the functional compensation upon rod death in P23H mice (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a conclusion about the most likely mechanisms based on the combined data.

claim: Care et al. proposed that functional compensation at rod bipolar cells upon ~50% input loss from rods was attributable to disinhibition.
source: On the other hand, Care et al. proposed that functional compensation at rod bipolar cells upon ~50% input loss from rods was attributable to disinhibition (our hypothesis 3).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: The mechanism by which neurons and neural networks adapt to acute stressors versus progressive disease conditions may differ.
source: It should be noted, however, that the mechanism by which neurons and neural networks adapt to acute stressors versus progressive disease conditions may differ.
evidence: This is a speculation about differences in adaptation mechanisms.

claim: It is possible that Müller cells would support bipolar cell function and contribute to the preservation of b-wave response amplitudes in ex vivo ERG experiments.
source: Another interesting possibility is that Müller cells would support bipolar cell function and contribute to the preservation of b-wave response amplitudes in ex vivo ERG experiments.
evidence: This is a speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: Although barium was used to block the slow PIII component, it is possible that Müller cells contribute to the ERG b-wave even in the presence of barium.
source: Although we used barium to block the slow PIII component (Bolnick et al., 1979), it is possible that Müller cells contribute to the ERG b-wave even in the presence of barium.
evidence: This is a speculation about a limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: If the Müller cell contribution to the b-wave changes in P23H mice, that could in principle also explain the observed potentiation of the ex vivo ERG b-waves in the P23H mice.
source: If this contribution changes in P23H mice, that could in principle also explain the observed potentiation of the ex vivo ERG b-waves in the P23H mice.
evidence: This is a speculation about an alternative explanation.

claim: Additional work will be needed to resolve the exact homeostatic plasticity mechanisms that promote rod-rod bipolar cell signaling and visual function.
source: Additional work will be needed to resolve the exact homeostatic plasticity mechanisms that promote rod-rod bipolar cell signaling and visual function.
evidence: This identifies a need for future research.

claim: Knowledge of homeostatic plasticity mechanisms could help us understand how sensory systems respond to potentially compromising circumstances throughout life, and as well help in designing interventions to enhance homeostatic plasticity when needed.
source: Such knowledge could then help us understand how sensory systems respond to potentially compromising circumstances throughout life, and as well help in designing interventions to enhance homeostatic plasticity when needed.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential impact of understanding these mechanisms.
